name: Pigmentation
summary: Melasma, sun spots and post-inflammatory marks each behave differently.
leadAnswer: Pigmentation describes areas of darker skin, most commonly sun spots, melasma and marks left after inflammation. They can look alike but are managed differently: sun spots are often treated with pico laser, melasma is managed conservatively and long-term, and post-inflammatory marks usually start with treating the cause.

facts.label: Melasma, sun spots and post-inflammatory marks look similar and behave differently.
The same laser that suits sun spots can aggravate melasma, so identification comes first.

facts.value: Sun protection is part of it
facts.label: Daily broad-spectrum sunscreen is included in every plan discussed here.

sections.heading: What is pigmentation?
body: Skin colour comes from melanin, made by cells called melanocytes. Pigmentation becomes a concern when melanin is produced or distributed unevenly, leaving patches darker than the surrounding skin.

drivers.heading: Common causes
drivers.intro: Usually more than one at once:

items.body: the most consistent contributor in a country with year-round equatorial UV. It both triggers new pigment and darkens what is already there, including through cloud and window glass.
pregnancy, hormonal contraception and thyroid conditions are all associated with melasma.

items.lead: Inflammation or injury to the skin:
items.body: acne, eczema, a burn, a cut or an aggressive cosmetic procedure can leave a flat brown mark behind as the skin settles. This is post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.
medium and deeper skin tones produce pigment more readily in response to injury, and melasma in particular tends to run in families.

variant.heading: Which type do I have?
variant.intro: These three account for most cases.

tabs.label: Sun spots
tabs.title: Sun-related pigmentation
tabs.body: Discrete, fairly well-defined brown patches on the areas that catch the most light. They accumulate slowly over years and do not fade in the way a tan does.

items.body: flat, evenly coloured brown spots with a clear border, often called age spots or sun spots.
smaller, lighter and more numerous, usually appearing early in life and darkening with sun exposure.

tabs.label: Melasma
tabs.title: Melasma
tabs.body: Larger, symmetrical patches with soft, ill-defined edges, typically across the cheeks, upper lip, forehead and jaw. It is hormone-influenced and heat-sensitive.

items.body: it darkens with sun, heat and hormonal shifts, and lightens again in quieter periods.

tabs.routing: assessed cautiously: conservative settings, longer intervals, daily protection.

tabs.label: Post-inflammatory
tabs.title: Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
tabs.body: Flat brown or grey-brown marks exactly where something happened: a spot, scratch, eczema or insect bite.

items.body: the shape of the mark matches whatever caused it, which is usually the clearest way to tell it apart from melasma.

items.lead: It often fades on its own:
items.body: though slowly, over months, and sun exposure prolongs it.

tabs.routing: settling the underlying cause first, then pico laser or supportive treatment if the mark persists.

locationBlock.heading: Where pigmentation appears
locationBlock.intro: Location is a clue rather than a diagnosis, but the pattern is often the first thing a doctor reads.

cards.title: Cheeks and cheekbones
cards.body: The most sun-exposed part of the face and the usual home of both sun spots and melasma. Symmetry across both cheeks points toward melasma; scattered discrete spots point away from it.

cards.title: Upper lip and jaw
cards.body: A symmetrical shadow above the lip or along the jaw is a common melasma pattern, and one that is often mistaken for facial hair or a shaving mark.

cards.title: Nose and bridge
cards.body: Catches direct light all day, so freckles and solar lentigines cluster here.

cards.title: Neck, chest and hands
cards.body: Frequently overlooked and frequently the most sun-damaged. Skin here is thinner, heals more slowly and is treated more conservatively than the face.

note.title: Not typical pigmentation?
note.body: A mark that is changing in size, shape or colour, has an irregular border, itches or bleeds should be examined promptly.

triggers: Over-the-counter brightening products have not helped after a few months of consistent use.
The patches are spreading, or returning each time they fade.
The pigmentation followed acne, eczema or a cosmetic procedure.

ctaMid.heading: Sun spots or melasma?
ctaMid.body: Send us a photo on WhatsApp and a doctor can tell you which you are looking at.

treatmentsIntro: Which one fits depends on the type:

pico-laser.why: For sun spots, freckles and stubborn pigment
pico-laser.body: A picosecond laser that shatters pigment with very short pulses rather than heating the surrounding skin.

vascular-pigment-laser.why: For redness sitting under the brown
vascular-pigment-laser.body: Targets both pigment and superficial blood vessels.

resurfacing-laser.why: For pigment bound up with texture change
resurfacing-laser.body: A fractional laser used where uneven tone sits alongside roughness, sun damage or scarring rather than on its own. More downtime.

skin-booster.why: For dull, dehydrated skin around the patches
skin-booster.body: Injectable hydration that addresses the overall quality of the skin rather than the pigment itself.

facial-treatments.why: For gentle exfoliation between laser sessions
facial-treatments.body: Hydrafacial and Silkpeel support surface cell turnover without the heat or aggression that aggravates melasma.

items.body: Redness, mild swelling, dryness and a gritty or warm sensation for a few days. Treated spots may darken and flake before they lift. Less common effects include blistering, prolonged redness or infection.

Medium and deeper skin tones carry a higher chance of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation after energy-based treatment: the exact problem being treated, made worse. This is why doctors here choose conservative settings and longer intervals, and why the course may run longer than you expect.
Treated too aggressively, melasma can darken rather than lighten, and that setback can take many months to settle.

No treatment changes the tendency to produce pigment. Melasma is managed rather than cured and commonly returns with sun, heat or hormonal change. Without daily sun protection, treated spots will not stay gone.

risks.disclose: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, taking hormonal contraception or hormone therapy, using retinoids or acids, have a history of cold sores or keloid scarring, have tanned recently, or have had any skin procedure in the past few weeks.

faqs.q: What is the difference between melasma and sun spots?
faqs.a: Sun spots are discrete brown patches with a fairly clear border. Melasma is larger, symmetrical and soft-edged, and it is influenced by hormones and heat as well as sun. They can look similar in a mirror and they are managed almost oppositely.
Because treatment addresses the pigment that is there, not the tendency to produce it. Daily sun protection and, where relevant, ongoing medical treatment are what keep treated skin stable.

faqs.q: Is laser safe for darker or Asian skin tones?
faqs.a: Yes, when the device and settings are chosen by a doctor experienced with your skin type. The specific risk in medium and deeper tones is post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation: the skin responding to treatment by producing more pigment. It is a real consideration rather than a reason to avoid treatment.

It is the single most consistent thing you can do, both to prevent new pigmentation and to hold on to any improvement. A broad-spectrum sunscreen applied every morning and reapplied through the day is standard advice, and tinted formulations add some protection against visible light, which is relevant in melasma.

faqs.q: Can pigmentation be treated during pregnancy?
faqs.a: Elective treatment is generally deferred until after pregnancy and breastfeeding. Melasma often appears or worsens during pregnancy because of hormonal change, and it commonly settles to some degree afterwards.
They can help with mild surface pigmentation and they support any in-clinic plan, but expectations should be modest. Where the pigment sits deeper, topical products alone often reach a ceiling.

faqs.q: Does the pigmentation get darker before it fades?
faqs.a: With some laser treatments, yes. Treated spots can appear darker for several days, then flake or lift as the skin turns over. This is an expected part of how the treatment works rather than a sign something has gone wrong.

faqs.q: Can I still use my retinol or acid products?
faqs.a: Do not stop or start anything without telling your doctor. Retinoids and exfoliating acids are usually paused for a period before and after energy-based treatment, because they thin the surface and increase sensitivity.
